title: What this means for energy traders — Tuesday, November 17, 2026

sections.overall: Today's news is dominated by one theme: a shift from supply scares toward surplus. The IEA says global oil supply has returned above demand for the first time since the Iran war began, as Gulf exports recover (CNBC). Security risks around Hormuz remain in the headlines, so signals are mixed. In carbon, COP31 is generating rules-and-infrastructure news rather than price news. I did not open full articles today; this summary relies on digest headlines and summaries.
sections.CRUDE_OIL: Headline-level coverage points to prices easing on surplus expectations. One aggregator report cites Brent at $91.71 and WTI at $84.94 (Gulf News via NewsData.io). Corporate activity continues in the other direction: Chevron's reported pursuit of Beacon Offshore (Financial Times) and ExxonMobil's Uaru start-up in Guyana (Offshore Energy) show majors adding supply. Usually, markets weigh a surplus reading against persistent shipping-security risk; which dominates is still unclear.
sections.NATURAL_GAS: LNG infrastructure stories cluster around import and export capacity: Woodfibre LNG funding in Canada, Shell's Malaysian gas start-up feeding Bintulu, and floating import terminals in Germany and Colombia. Asset sales such as NRG's gas plants to LS Power and Sempra's stake sale to a KKR-led group show capital reshuffling. Utility and regulatory items, like Duke Energy's order in North Carolina, tie gas to power demand. Several are company press releases, so treat them with care.
sections.REFINED_PRODUCTS: Heating oil costs are a consumer story: the Guardian reports a projected 21% increase for heating oil households (The Guardian). US diesel fell below $6 a gallon for the first time in two months per aggregator reports. Supply-side risk persists through Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, and Russian diesel flows have shifted after sanctions changes. The interaction between these is unresolved.
sections.CARBON_CREDITS: COP31 produced the first version of the Article 6.2 international registry and EU rules on crediting carbon prices paid abroad under CBAM. Such institutional steps are usually read as improving market plumbing and clarity, though effects on demand are gradual. EU carbon prices were little changed Tuesday, up 8 cents (Carbon Pulse).
